summary: Defines PANA, a network-layer transport for EAP that lets clients authenticate to an access network. In EAP terms it is a UDP-based lower layer between the EAP peer and the authenticator. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: PANA carries EAP authentication messages between a client and an access network over IP. It manages the exchange and can protect later messages with a key derived during EAP authentication.

questions: eap over udp for network access
protocol for carrying authentication for network access
what are the phases of a pana session
subtitle: A UDP-based transport for EAP authentication between a client and an access network.

tldr.problem: A network needs a way to carry authentication between a client and an access network without depending on a particular link technology.
tldr.mechanism: PANA carries EAP messages between a PANA Client and PANA Authentication Agent over UDP. Sequence numbers and retransmissions support reliable delivery; an EAP-derived key can protect messages.
tldr.outcome: PANA provides authentication transport, not discovery, access-filter setup, or data-traffic protection. RFC 5191 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 5872.

today: RFC 5191 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2008. The unit metadata says it was updated by RFC 5872.

sections.title: A Transport for Network Access Authentication
sections.content:
The Protocol for Carrying Authentication for Network Access (PANA) carries the Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) between an access device and an access network. It runs above IP, so it can carry EAP methods over different link technologies.

PANA does not specify every part of a network-access solution. Agent discovery, authentication-method choice, communication with enforcement points, access filters, and protection of data traffic are outside this protocol specification.
sections.plainLanguage: PANA transports EAP messages between a client and an access network. Other protocols and components handle agent discovery and control of the client's data traffic.

sections.title: The Client, Agent and Session
sections.content:
The PANA Client (PaC) runs in the access device and provides credentials. The PANA Authentication Agent (PAA) verifies them and authorizes network access; it may use a back-end authentication, authorization, and accounting system.

An Enforcement Point applies per-packet filters and should block data traffic from unauthorized clients, while allowing PANA and selected network-control traffic. A PANA session joins one PaC and one PAA, has an identifier assigned by the PAA, and is not shared across network interfaces.
sections.plainLanguage: The client provides credentials, the agent verifies them, and an enforcement point applies the resulting access rules. One PANA session links a client with an agent.

sections.title: The Four Session Phases
sections.content:
Authentication and authorization starts a session and carries EAP messages. Either the client or agent may initiate it. The agent reports the result in the final request, which the client acknowledges.

During the access phase, either peer may send a ping to test whether the other is responding. Re-authentication runs EAP again to extend authorization. Either side can end the session with a termination request, after which session state is removed when the request is acknowledged.
sections.plainLanguage: PANA first authenticates and authorizes the client, then allows network access. The peers can test liveness, repeat authentication before authorization expires, or terminate the session.

sections.title: Sequence Numbers and Retransmission
sections.content:
PANA uses separate 32-bit sequence numbers for outgoing requests and expected incoming requests. A request increases the number by one, wrapping after 2^32 - 1; its answer repeats that request's number. Each peer can have only one outstanding request.

A sender retransmits a request until it receives an answer or reaches its retry limit. The peers must answer duplicate requests unless rate limiting drops them. PANA does not define its own fragmentation and relies on EAP methods and IP when fragmentation is needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Sequence numbers let a peer match each answer to its request and reject messages that arrive unexpectedly. Retransmission lets a request be sent again if its answer does not arrive.

sections.title: Messages and Attribute-Value Pairs
sections.content:
PANA messages are unicast between the PaC and PAA over UDP port 716. A header contains message length, flags, message type, a 32-bit session identifier, and a 32-bit sequence number. Flags identify requests, session start and completion, re-authentication, ping, and IP reconfiguration.

Attribute-value pairs (AVPs) carry items such as EAP payloads, nonces, algorithm choices, results, and session lifetime. The AVP code identifies the attribute and its length describes the value.
sections.plainLanguage: Each PANA message identifies its session, sequence number, and message type. AVPs carry the authentication data and other information needed for that exchange.

sections.title: Protecting Messages with an EAP Key
sections.content:
If EAP produces a Master Session Key, PANA derives a PANA authentication key from it and session values. An AUTH AVP carries a message authentication code that covers the PANA message, including its header and payload.

Once the key is available, messages carrying EAP success and later messages must include valid authentication information. A new key from re-authentication replaces the old key for subsequent messages.
sections.plainLanguage: When EAP produces a shared key, PANA derives a session key and uses it to check message integrity and authenticity. The check helps the receiver reject altered or forged messages.

sections.title: Security Limits
sections.content:
The initial exchange is not authenticated, so an attacker may spoof its messages. The PAA should create as little state as possible in response to a client initiation. Sequence numbers help reject stale or unexpected messages, and an EAP-derived key can protect subsequent PANA messages.

Weak EAP methods may expose passwords or identities. Operators and users are responsible for choosing an appropriate EAP method. Frequent ping messages can also cause congestion and false liveness alarms.
sections.plainLanguage: The first exchange can be spoofed, so the agent limits the state it creates before authentication. Later protection depends on the EAP method producing suitable keys.
